newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Marine medicine research filled with potential, risk.
newsitem.headline: Marine medicine research filled with potential, risk.

text.p: The oceans may harbour cures for what ails us but finding new drugs in the sea is a risky, costly process with no guarantee of success, marine researchers say.

Using advanced undersea exploration equipment that allows them to go where no scientist has gone before, prospectors are scouring the seas in search of unique chemical compounds from some of Earth's most creative creatures. Researchers and pharmaceutical firms are putting marine-made oddities to work as possible cures for ills ranging from cancer and AIDS to arthritis, hair loss and puffy eyes.

"No matter how creative a chemist can be ... nature is much more creative," Dr. Shirley Pomponi, director of Biomedical Marine Research at the Harbour Branch Oceanographic Institution in Fort Pierce, Florida, explained.

On a recent exploration in the Bahamas, Harbour Branch researchers used a small submarine to collect dozens of samples of algae, sponges and sea fans to be run through hundreds of random tests for possible use in drugs. Scientists say the sheer volume of ocean life -- thousands of species of sponge and algae and "millions and millions" of microscopic sea organisms -- holds the promise of new remedies.

The peculiarities of predators, pressure and salinity prod sea organisms to manufacture unique toxic chemicals for self-defence. Creation of those chemicals, known as "natural products," mimics the manufacture by coffee plants of caffeine, which scientists think was created as a pesticide.

Harbour Branch alone has about 75 patents from marine sources. A group of compounds dubbed the topsentins, isolated from a mustard-yellow sponge, may be good anti-inflammatories for arthritis, facial swelling or sunburn, Pomponi said.

A compound called discodermolide was found in a hard, pale sponge found 500-700 feet (152-213 metres) deep in the Caribbean. First touted as an immune suppressant, the chemical is now hailed as a cancer-fighter that could rival taxol, the breakthrough cancer drug derived from the Pacific yew tree.
"Taxol has some side effects we think the dermolide might not have," Pomponi said. In tests, discodermolide has shown promise against ovarian, breast and lung cancers.

But the search for new marine compounds can be a long and financially perilous quest, said Bill Fenical of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography near San Diego, California. Most drugs take at least 10 years from discovery to production, during which the compound could be overtaken by better drugs or fail due to late-developing side effects.
"It's really risky. It's big potential profits but big potential losses," Fenical said. The rewards can be huge. Drugs often ring up sales of $200-600 million annually.

Scripps developed a chemical, pseudopterosin, an anti-inflammatory to keep down facial swelling, from a marine animal called a sea whip that is being used in a line of Estee Lauder cosmetics called "Resilience," Fenical said.

One of the most promising sea chemicals is ecteinascidia, found in an invertebrate called the sea squirt. Now in clinical trials for PharmaMar, a Spanish company, the compound can kill melanoma, one of the most lethal cancers.

But its promise illustrates a troubling aspect of marine-based drugs -- mass production. It takes a tonne of sea squirts to produce a gram of ecteinascidia, stirring fears of over-harvesting of wild organisms.
"It may be a big constraint in the development of this field," Dr. Donald de Sylva, a marine biology professor at the University of Miami, said.

Pharmaceutical companies prefer to synthesize the chemical or reproduce it by cell- or aqua-culture. "It would be the kiss of death if a pharmaceutical company thinks it can't get enough to market the drug," Pomponi said.

Searching for mass production methods, Harbour Branch researchers discovered that a flatworm that feeds on the sea squirt can isolate and store ecteinascidia without killing the squirt. The compound can then be "milked" from the flatworm.

Pharmaceutical industry officials say marine medical research remains a relatively small part of the industry because most drug companies concentrate on genetic engineering and synthesis of new drugs. But many firms have a hand in marine research because of the potential for a blockbuster.
"The blockbuster would be a cure for cancer. Or a cure for AIDS," Pomponi said.
